marks: Jesus of Nazareth was crucified here under Pontius Pilate around 30; his followers proclaimed his resurrection.
Where the followers of Jesus were first called Christians.
By tradition Peter and Paul died here under Nero; the bishops of Rome became the popes.
By tradition Armenia became the first state to adopt Christianity (301); its mother cathedral stands here.
Constantine called the first council of the whole church here in 325; it defined the Nicene Creed.
Constantine's new capital (330), the centre of Eastern Christianity; Hagia Sophia was rebuilt under Justinian (537).
King Ezana of Aksum adopted Christianity in the 4th century.
Columba founded the monastery of Iona in 563.
Augustine's mission from Rome arrived in 597.
The Xi'an Stele (781) records the Church of the East in China since 635.
Vladimir of Kiev was baptised and his people with him (around 988).
Pope Gregory VII wrote to the archbishop of Carthage in 1076; by the 12th century native Christianity had died out in North Africa.
Gravestones of the Church of the East here run to the 1340s; Christianity disappeared from Central Asia by the end of the 14th century.
The capital of Christian Makuria; its throne hall became a mosque in 1317, and the Nubian kingdoms' Christianity faded by about 1500.
Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517) began the Protestant Reformation.
The Spanish settlement of Cebu (1565) began the conversion of the Philippines.
Japan's hidden Christians kept their faith in secret for over two centuries, until the ban was lifted in 1873.
The Greek Orthodox of Cappadocia, Christians here since the 1st century, left in the population exchange of 1923.
notes: Jesus of Nazareth is crucified in Jerusalem around 30; his followers proclaim him the Messiah, and Paul carries the message to Gentiles across the eastern Mediterranean.
Christian communities spread through the cities of the Roman Empire, from Syria and Egypt to Rome, Gaul and North Africa; the New Testament takes shape.
The churches grow despite persecution under Decius (250) and Valerian; Christianity reaches Mesopotamia and Persia.
Constantine ends the persecution (313) and calls the Council of Nicaea (325); Armenia, Georgia and Aksum adopt Christianity; Theodosius makes it the religion of the empire (380).
Patrick preaches in Ireland; the councils of Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) divide the churches of the East; Rome falls (476) but its bishops remain.
Justinian rebuilds Hagia Sophia (537); the Nubian kingdoms are converted; Augustine's mission reaches England (597).
Arab armies conquer Syria, Egypt and Persia, where Christians remain the majority for centuries; the Church of the East reaches Tang China (635).
Muslim armies take most of Spain (711); Boniface preaches in Germany, and Charlemagne forces the Saxons to convert.
Cyril and Methodius bring the liturgy to the Slavs (863); Bulgaria is baptised (864).
Poland (966), Kievan Rus' (988) and Denmark turn to Christianity; Iceland adopts it around 1000.
The Great Schism divides the Latin West from the Greek East (1054); the First Crusade takes Jerusalem (1099); Norway and Sweden become Christian.
Native Christianity dies out in North Africa; in Spain the Christian kingdoms push south; the Church of the East spreads among the Turkic and Mongol peoples.
Mongol rule opens Asia to missionaries, and Franciscans reach Beijing (1294); the last Crusader states fall (1291).
Lithuania, the last pagan state of Europe, is baptised (1387); in Central Asia and China the Church of the East disappears.
The Ottomans take Constantinople (1453); the Portuguese baptise the king of Kongo (1491); Columbus reaches the Americas (1492).
Luther's theses (1517) begin the Reformation; Spain and Portugal carry Catholicism to the Americas, Goa, Japan and the Philippines.
Japan bans Christianity (1614); Puritans settle New England (1620); Jesuits work in China and New France.
Methodism and the Great Awakening spread revival; the first Korean Catholics are baptised (1784); British settlers bring their churches to Australia (1788).
Missionaries travel across Africa, Asia and the Pacific; Christianity becomes a main faith of Madagascar, much of Polynesia and southern Africa.
Christianity grows fast in Africa, Korea and China and declines in much of Europe; the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) reforms the Catholic Church.
About 2.3 billion Christians (2020): the largest religion in the world, with the most followers now in sub-Saharan Africa.
src: Diarmaid MacCulloch, A History of Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years (2009)
